For press releases and other information of interest to investors, please visit Cohu's website at www.cohu.com.

Luis A. Muller, President & CEO of Cohu, Inc. (COHU +4.46%), sold 55,794 shares of common stock on Sept. 21, 2026, according to a SEC Form 4 filing.
Post-transaction shares (directly held)871,825
Transaction value based on SEC Form 4 weighted average sale price ($60.00); post-transaction value based on Sept. 21, 2026, market close ($60.62).
How does this transaction relate to the CEO's total equity position?
The disposal of 55,794 shares represents a 6% portion of the stake held by Luis A. Muller before the filing. After the sale, the insider maintains a direct holding of 871,825 shares, which includes 508,101 restricted stock units that convert to common stock upon vesting.
What was the market context at the time of the transaction?
Shares of the semiconductor equipment company have appreciated 169% over the 12 months ending on the transaction date. The shares were sold at $60.00 per share, while the market closed at $60.62 on the same day.
What is the purpose of the Rule 10b5-1 trading plan?
The plan, adopted on May 28, 2026, allows insiders to establish pre-determined trading instructions for future dates. This mechanism enables executives to manage equity compensation and personal liquidity on a scheduled basis, regardless of subsequent stock price movements.
Share Price (as of market close 2026-09-22)$64.54

The company generates revenue through the sale of proprietary test equipment and the provision of related services to semiconductor manufacturers and test subcontractors, leveraging its technological expertise to address complex testing requirements in the semiconductor industry.
Cohu serves a global customer base of semiconductor and electronics manufacturers, as well as independent test subcontractors, with significant operational presence across key markets including the United States, China, Taiwan, Malaysia, and the Philippines.
$3.5BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.

The company has demonstrated significant market momentum, with a one-year share price appreciation of 169%, reflecting investor confidence in the semiconductor testing equipment sector. Despite current net losses of $39 million on a TTM basis, Cohu maintains substantial TTM revenue of $523 million, positioning the company as a significant participant in the specialized semiconductor equipment market.
What this transaction means for investors
This sale shouldn't concern investors. It was executed under a preplanned trading schedule, and the transaction represented a small percentage of the executive's stock holdings.
Importantly, Cohu is experiencing robust growth, with TTM revenue surging 33% year over year. The growing demand has narrowed its operating loss to -$36 million on a same-basis, down from -$70 million in 2025.
The stock has recently been volatile after a sharp increase. It trades at a forward P/E of 44, while analysts still expect earnings to grow at an annualized rate of 20% in the coming years.

The week after I deleted it, I received a message from that department saying their monthly report was empty, and I had to scramble to restore it.
It was then that I realized for the first time that input rates and report reference counts alone cannot capture usage that doesn't appear on the screen, such as Flow conditional branches or report filter criteria.

The story of how I used AI to identify 47 unused Salesforce custom fields that had been accumulating unnoticed for years | Sharing the prompts I used
Every time I opened the Salesforce object setup screen, there was something that bothered me a little.
There are just so many fields.
Both Contacts and Opportunities are lined with custom fields with labels I've never heard of.
Someone must have added them because they needed them, but whenever I ask any of the current team members, the only response I get is, 'What was this used for again?'
In many cases, the people who knew the circumstances at the time were no longer on the team due to past transfers or resignations.
I imagine many of you have felt the same frustration when faced with a similar screen.
As an engineering manager, I have always wanted to clean up this situation.
However, to be honest, I kept putting it off.
Developing new features and fixing bugs seem to have higher priority, and cleaning up fields is a tedious task that doesn't contribute to anyone's performance evaluation.
Even so, the reason I finally decided to take action was that it took nearly half a day just to explain the screen when a new member joined the company.
Watching the back-and-forth of 'Are you using this?' and 'I think we're probably not using it' repeated dozens of times, I felt that this was no longer a situation that could rely on individual memory.
So, I decided to have AI help me with the field inventory.
If I had relied only on my own memory to check them one by one, I'm sure the day would have ended before I finished.
In this article, I will summarize the prompts I actually sent to the AI, the number of unused fields found as a result, and the perspectives I made sure to check before deleting them.
I hope this will be a reference for those who, like me, have a vague anxiety about the number of fields in a Salesforce organization that has been in operation for many years.
When I had AI summarize the usage status, 47 unused fields were found
The first thing I did was to export the list of fields for each object and the reference status in reports and list views for the last year.
Salesforce itself has a mechanism to check field usage, but trying to list them across objects takes a considerable amount of effort on its own.
So, I passed the exported data to the AI and made the following request.
Looking at the list that came back, I was surprised at the sheer number at first.
There were 47 fields with an input rate of almost zero that had never even been used in a report.
There were over a dozen in the Account object alone, and about the same number in the Opportunity object.
Honestly, some of them were fields I didn't even remember seeing once since I joined the company.
I learned the hard way during my first deletion attempt that "safe to delete" and "can be deleted" are two different things.
Just because I knew the number didn't mean I could delete them all at once.
At first, I was going to proceed with deleting them in order, starting with the fields that had a zero input rate, without much verification.
One of those fields turned out to be used in the extraction criteria for an old report used only by a specific department.
The week after I deleted it, I received a message from that department saying their monthly report was empty, and I had to scramble to restore it.
It was then that I realized for the first time that input rates and report reference counts alone cannot capture usage that doesn't appear on the screen, such as Flow conditional branches or report filter criteria.
After this failure, I made it a rule to have AI perform an extra check before any deletion.

I imagine many of you have felt the same frustration when faced with a similar screen.
As an engineering manager, I have always wanted to clean up this situation.
However, to be honest, I kept putting it off.
Developing new features and fixing bugs seem to have higher priority, and cleaning up fields is a tedious task that doesn't contribute to anyone's performance evaluation.
Even so, the reason I finally decided to take action was that it took nearly half a day just to explain the screen when a new member joined the company.
Watching the back-and-forth of 'Are you using this?' and 'I think we're probably not using it' repeated dozens of times, I felt that this was no longer a situation that could rely on individual memory.
So, I decided to have AI help me with the field inventory.
If I had relied only on my own memory to check them one by one, I'm sure the day would have ended before I finished.
In this article, I will summarize the prompts I actually sent to the AI, the number of unused fields found as a result, and the perspectives I made sure to check before deleting them.
I hope this will be a reference for those who, like me, have a vague anxiety about the number of fields in a Salesforce organization that has been in operation for many years.
When I had AI summarize the usage status, 47 unused fields were found
The first thing I did was to export the list of fields for each object and the reference status in reports and list views for the last year.
Salesforce itself has a mechanism to check field usage, but trying to list them across objects takes a considerable amount of effort on its own.
So, I passed the exported data to the AI and made the following request.
Looking at the list that came back, I was surprised at the sheer number at first.
There were 47 fields with an input rate of almost zero that had never even been used in a report.
There were over a dozen in the Account object alone, and about the same number in the Opportunity object.
Honestly, some of them were fields I didn't even remember seeing once since I joined the company.
I learned the hard way during my first deletion attempt that "safe to delete" and "can be deleted" are two different things.
Just because I knew the number didn't mean I could delete them all at once.
At first, I was going to proceed with deleting them in order, starting with the fields that had a zero input rate, without much verification.
One of those fields turned out to be used in the extraction criteria for an old report used only by a specific department.
The week after I deleted it, I received a message from that department saying their monthly report was empty, and I had to scramble to restore it.
It was then that I realized for the first time that input rates and report reference counts alone cannot capture usage that doesn't appear on the screen, such as Flow conditional branches or report filter criteria.
After this failure, I made it a rule to have AI perform an extra check before any deletion.

The story of how I used AI to identify 47 unused Salesforce custom fields that had been accumulating unnoticed for years | Sharing the prompts I used
Every time I opened the Salesforce object setup screen, there was something that bothered me a little.
There are just so many fields.
Both Contacts and Opportunities are lined with custom fields with labels I've never heard of.
Someone must have added them because they needed them, but whenever I ask any of the current team members, the only response I get is, 'What was this used for again?'
In many cases, the people who knew the circumstances at the time were no longer on the team due to past transfers or resignations.
I imagine many of you have felt the same frustration when faced with a similar screen.
As an engineering manager, I have always wanted to clean up this situation.
However, to be honest, I kept putting it off.
Developing new features and fixing bugs seem to have higher priority, and cleaning up fields is a tedious task that doesn't contribute to anyone's performance evaluation.
Even so, the reason I finally decided to take action was that it took nearly half a day just to explain the screen when a new member joined the company.
Watching the back-and-forth of 'Are you using this?' and 'I think we're probably not using it' repeated dozens of times, I felt that this was no longer a situation that could rely on individual memory.
So, I decided to have AI help me with the field inventory.
If I had relied only on my own memory to check them one by one, I'm sure the day would have ended before I finished.
In this article, I will summarize the prompts I actually sent to the AI, the number of unused fields found as a result, and the perspectives I made sure to check before deleting them.
I hope this will be a reference for those who, like me, have a vague anxiety about the number of fields in a Salesforce organization that has been in operation for many years.
